St. Mary's Glacier

memories below

Copper Sky

One Saturday in mid-August, the sky changed color. Wildfires were burning in western Colorado, and westerly winds had pushed their smoke all the way to the Front Range. Around noon, from a roadside viewpoint south of Georgetown, the sky was still mostly blue, but the far ridges had already faded into haze. A power line cut a straight stripe through the forest down the valley. I had a glacier to get to!

St. Mary's Glacier is a short hike from a trailhead about nine miles up Fall River Road from I-70 at Idaho Springs. By a little before four in the afternoon, the light on the trail already looked like sunset. Magenta fireweed crowded the path beside a bleached, gnarled old tree, a loud pink against all that orange. The plant is named for how readily it moves into burned ground, which felt a little too fitting under that sky. Strictly speaking, St. Mary's is a perennial snowfield, too thin to flow the way a true glacier does, but it looks the part: a wide, rippled slope of old snow, streaked with dust and grit. The dog didn't care about the distinction. It plowed nose-first through the snow in its red pack like a furry bulldozer. Up in the haze, the sun was just a dim orange dot.

On Sunday I flew west out of Denver, and the window showed me how big the smoke really was. Milky layers of it were stacked over the valleys, a plume climbed out of the hills like a thunderhead, and above it all the sky was a clean, deep blue. Far below, a tiny jet crossed the haze.

A perennial snowfield is supposed to outlast every summer, but news reports say St. Mary's melted out completely in September 2026. I'm glad I saw it, copper sky and all.
